title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part Three: Message Header Extensions for Non-ASCII Text
summary: The third MIME document. It extends the older email message format to let non-ASCII text appear in header fields, such as names and subjects, using an encoding that older systems can still carry.

plainLanguage.summary: It teaches email to put accented letters and other alphabets in the subject line by disguising them as plain letters.

questions: how to put non-ascii text in email headers
what are encoded words in mime
what is an encoded word in email
what is the difference between q and b encoding
how long can an encoded word be
subtitle: How non-ASCII text such as accented names and subjects is smuggled through email headers as plain printable ASCII.

tldr.problem: RFC 822 email headers are US-ASCII only, yet people want names and subjects in other character sets, and existing mail software can mangle anything unusual.
tldr.mechanism: Non-ASCII text is wrapped in an encoded-word of the form =?charset?encoding?encoded-text?=, using only ordinary printable ASCII, with either the Q or B encoding. It may appear only in certain places in a header.
tldr.outcome: Mail readers recognise encoded-words and show the original text, while old software just sees harmless ASCII. RFC 2047 obsoletes RFC 1521, 1522 and 1590 and has been updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 2047 is listed as a Draft Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 2184 and RFC 2231. It replaced RFC 1521, RFC 1522 and RFC 1590.

sections.title: Non-ASCII Text in Headers
sections.content:
This is the third document in the MIME series. RFC 2045 covers body parts in other character sets; RFC 2047 does the same kind of job for the message header, in a way unlikely to confuse existing software. It does not define any translation between 8-bit headers and pure ASCII headers.

The caution is deliberate. The RFC notes that some relays delete some header fields, reorder addresses, reorder fields or wrap lines in new places, and some readers trip over legal but obscure RFC 822 tricks like backslash-quoting. So the design avoids rarely used features. Instead, certain sequences of ordinary printable ASCII, called encoded-words, are reserved for encoded data, and their syntax is unlikely to appear by accident.

A composing program turns non-ASCII text into encoded-words before inserting it into the header. A reader recognises them, reverses the encoding and shows the text in the named character set.
sections.plainLanguage: Old mail machines only understand plain letters. So we write fancy letters in a secret code made of plain letters, and the receiving computer turns the code back into fancy letters.

sections.title: The Encoded-Word Syntax
sections.content:
An encoded-word is =? charset ? encoding ? encoded-text ?=, with no white space between the parts. Charset and encoding are tokens, and their names are case-independent, so Q and q are the same. The encoded-text is printable ASCII other than ? and SPACE.

An encoded-word may not be longer than 75 characters, counting the charset, encoding, text and delimiters. For longer text, use several encoded-words separated by CRLF SPACE. Each line of a header containing an encoded-word is limited to 76 characters. The limits ease passage through gateways and bound how far a parser must look ahead for the closing ?=.

Encoded-words must look like an RFC 822 atom, so unencoded SPACE and TAB are forbidden inside. Writing =?iso-8859-1?q?this is some text?= would parse as four atoms. The correct form encodes the spaces: =?iso-8859-1?q?this=20is=20some=20text?=.
sections.plainLanguage: The coded piece has a start sign, a note saying which alphabet it uses, a note saying which code it uses, the coded message and an end sign. It must not be too long, and it cannot contain spaces.

sections.title: Character Sets and the Q and B Encodings
sections.content:
The charset can be any name allowed in the MIME charset parameter of a text/plain body part or registered with IANA for that type. If a character set uses code-switching away from ASCII mode, the text MUST include the control codes to return to ASCII at the end of each encoded-word. Without a private agreement, the ISO-8859-* series is recommended when more than one set would work.

Two encodings exist. The B encoding is identical to the BASE64 encoding of RFC 2045. The Q encoding is similar to Quoted-Printable and is meant to stay readable on an ASCII terminal. Q is recommended when most characters are ASCII; otherwise B should be used. Readers that claim to support encoded-words MUST accept either encoding for any character set they support.

In Q, any 8-bit value can be written as = and two upper-case hex digits, so SPACE is =20. The underscore _ always means hex 20. Printable ASCII characters other than =, ? and _ MAY stand for themselves, but SPACE and TAB MUST NOT.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to write the code. One keeps most plain letters as they are and only changes the fancy ones. The other scrambles everything into a block of letters and numbers.

sections.title: Where Encoded-Words May Appear
sections.content:
Encoded-words may appear in only three kinds of places. First, in place of text in a Subject or Comments field, in extension fields, in MIME body part fields defined as *text, and in user-defined X- fields. Second, inside a parenthesised comment of a structured field. Third, as a replacement for a word in a phrase, such as the display name before an address in From, To or Cc. Within a phrase, a Q-encoded word is restricted to ASCII letters, digits and a short list of punctuation characters, including the underscore.

Everywhere else they are forbidden: not in any part of an addr-spec, not within a quoted-string, not in Received, not in MIME Content-Type or Content-Disposition parameters, and not in other structured field bodies. An encoded-word must be separated from adjacent text or encoded-words by linear white space.

Each encoded-word must be self-contained: it encodes a whole number of octets and a whole number of characters, so a multi-octet character cannot be split across two. Only printable text should be encoded, and encoding purely ASCII text is allowed but discouraged.
sections.plainLanguage: The code is allowed in the subject line and in people's names, but never in the email address itself, because the post office needs to read the address exactly.

sections.title: How Mail Readers Handle Them
sections.content:
Readers parse headers by RFC 822 rules and then look for encoded-words. In *text and user-defined fields, each run of up to 75 printable characters after white space is checked against the syntax. In other fields, a word within a phrase is treated as an encoded-word if it fits the syntax, and the same goes for sequences inside comments. A MIME-Version header is not required for decoding.

Recognised words are decoded and displayed in their original character set where possible. White space between two adjacent encoded-words is ignored for display, so long text can be split without worrying about where spaces fall. A space that should show must be encoded inside a word. Decoding happens after parsing, so special characters can be hidden inside encoded-words, and a header with encoded-words generally cannot be translated back into plain RFC 822 form.

If the reader does not know the encoding or charset, it may show the raw encoded-word, do its best, or substitute a message. A malformed encoded-word need not be displayed, but a reader MUST NOT refuse to display or handle a message because of one.
sections.plainLanguage: When a reader sees the coded piece, it decodes it and shows the real letters. If the code is broken, it just skips it and still shows the rest of the letter.

sections.title: Conformance Requirements
sections.content:
A composing program that claims compliance MUST make sure any run of non-white-space printable ASCII within *text or *ctext that begins with =? and ends with ?= is a valid encoded-word. The same holds for any word in a phrase. So ordinary text that happens to look like an encoded-word must itself be encoded.

A reading program that claims compliance must tell encoded-words from ordinary text according to the reader rules, and must support both B and Q for any character set it supports. It must be able to display US-ASCII text, and for the ISO-8859-* sets it must at least display the characters that are also in ASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: If you write something that looks like the secret code, it has to be a real, working code. And a reader that says it understands the code must really handle both kinds.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows names such as =?ISO-8859-1?Q?Keld_J=F8rn_Simonsen?= in a To field, where _ is a space and =F8 is the character with that ISO-8859-1 code. A Subject is split into two B-encoded words with different charsets; the trailing = in the first is needed because each word must be self-contained.

A table of comment examples shows the display rules: (=?ISO-8859-1?Q?a?= =?ISO-8859-1?Q?b?=) shows as (ab), because white space between adjacent encoded-words is dropped, while (=?ISO-8859-1?Q?a_b?=) shows as (a b), because the space was encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how the coded names look in a real letter and how the reader turns them back into proper names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.

Elsewhere the text does give two related cautions. Because decoding happens after parsing, special characters can be hidden in encoded-words and then look the same as real ones when displayed. And since the schemes can encode any octet value, readers should ensure that showing the decoded data will not have unwanted side effects on the recipient's terminal.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not talk about safety, but it warns readers to be careful about what the decoded letters might do on the screen.

data.title: encoded-word ABNF
data.code:
encoded-word = "=?" charset "?" encoding "?" encoded-text "?="

charset = token    ; see section 3

encoding = token   ; see section 4

encoded-text = 1*<Any printable ASCII character other than "?"
                  or SPACE>
